methodology.text:
Disordered Eating Patient — Curation Methodology
Companion to Patient_Profile.docx. Explains exactly how each data layer in this folder was produced, in the same spirit as 1- CKD/CKD_Patient_Curation_Methodology.docx.
1. Wearable layer — LifeSnaps participant selection
Source: Aamrut/lifesnaps/csv_rais_anonymized/daily_fitbit_sema_df_unprocessed.csv and Aamrut/lifesnaps/mongo_rais_anonymized/ (71 anonymized participants, Fitbit Sense, ~4 months each). Preprocessing follows the LifeSnaps-EDA notebook: https://github.com/Datalab-AUTH/LifeSnaps-EDA/blob/main/notebooks_preprocessing/visualization_df_creation.ipynb
Participant id: 621e351a67b776a240f6204b
Selection signal: hourly-resolution data was checked specifically for late-night (11PM–3AM) movement — ~60% of this participant’s late-night hours show non-zero steps with elevated heart rate, the strongest "awake and active at night" signal of any qualifying participant in the 71-person pool. Also has the lowest, most variable sleep efficiency (82–91%) and shortest sleep duration in the pool.
Window: 2021-05-27 → 2021-08-24, a completely gap-free 90-day window.
Modification applied: none — every physiological value in the CSVs is untouched, real device data. Only the choice of participant and window was steered toward this narrative.
2. Clinical layer — Synthea FHIR generation + hand-authored entries
Synthea (src/main/resources/modules/, 107 modules at time of generation) has no module for eating disorders, night-eating syndrome, or generalized anxiety disorder — confirmed by searching all module filenames and the anxiety-related content that does exist (only a GAD-7 *screening* sub-module inside encounter/anxiety_screening.json, not a diagnosable-condition module). Unlike Profile 1 (Hypothyroidism), where a real Synthea module could be run to produce the diagnosis, this profile required a different, explicitly-flagged approach.
Command used for the base patient: run_synthea -g M -a 25-27 -s 303 -p 40 --exporter.baseDirectory=./output_disordered/ Massachusetts (no -m filter — a general-population run, so the base record is an ordinary, non-targeted Synthea patient).
Candidate chosen: Nathan164 Randolph418 Schaden604 (male, born 2000-08-09 — 26 years old as of "today," matching the narrative age exactly), selected from the 40-patient pool for having the lowest count of unrelated chronic/notable conditions (only childhood perennial allergic rhinitis, resolved by 2019) so the hand-authored anxiety/night-eating layer would not have to compete with an unrelated, conflicting clinical picture.
Hand-authored Condition: Generalized anxiety disorder, coded with the standard, real-world SNOMED CT code 21897009 ("Generalized anxiety disorder (disorder)"), the same coding system Synthea itself uses throughout its output. Dated 2022-10-26 by anchoring to this patient’s own real Synthea-simulated check-up encounter on that date, so the new Condition references a genuine Encounter resource already in the bundle rather than inventing one.
Hand-authored MedicationRequest: Mirtazapine 15 MG Oral Tablet, coded with RxNorm CUI 351249, the standard real-world code for this exact strength/form. Dated 2025-12-29, anchored to this patient’s own real encounter-for-symptom on that date.
Transparency mechanism: both hand-authored resources carry an explicit FHIR `note` field stating "NOT Synthea-simulated: hand-authored ... because Synthea has no [X] module" — so anyone parsing the JSON directly, without reading this document, still hits a clear in-line disclosure. No other resource in the bundle was added, removed, or edited; the remaining 35 encounters and their conditions/immunizations/claims are Synthea’s raw, unmodified output.
3. Why the two layers do not share an identity
Same convention as Profile 1 and as 1- CKD itself: the clinical-layer Synthea patient (Nathan Schaden) and the wearable-layer LifeSnaps participant + narrative ("Theo") are two separate sources. Here the ages happen to land close (both ~26), which is a curation choice (see selection criteria above), not a guarantee — do not assume this holds for the other two profiles in this project, where the ages diverge on purpose.

limitations.text:
Limitations — Disordered Eating Profile
Read before drawing conclusions from this profile. As in 1- CKD/Limitations.docx: the profile narrative is the source of truth for "what this profile represents," not the CSV or JSON alone.
Limitations specific to the hand-authored clinical entries
The GAD diagnosis and mirtazapine prescription are not Synthea-simulated. They were manually authored using standard, real SNOMED CT (21897009) and RxNorm (351249) codes because no Synthea module models either condition or medication. They are internally consistent with valid FHIR structure and reference real encounters already in the underlying simulation, but they were never produced or validated by Synthea’s clinical-progression engine the way the rest of the bundle was. Both resources carry an in-line `note` field disclosing this.
The eating-disorder history and night-eating pattern exist only in the narrative text, not in any FHIR resource at all. There is no eating-disorder Condition in the JSON — Fitbit/Synthea have no way to represent it, and inventing a formal eating-disorder diagnosis code risked overstating clinical precision this profile does not have. If a system under test is expected to "find" the eating-disorder history, it can only do so from Patient_Profile.docx / the original profile_2_disordered_eating.md — not from the JSON.
Fitbit does not detect eating. The "night eating" framing is inferred entirely from late-night (11PM–3AM) movement and heart rate; the raw signal only shows this participant is awake and physically active at night, which could equally reflect insomnia, anxiety, or unrelated nocturnal habits.
Three different date regimes are stacked in this folder: the wearable CSVs use real 2021-05 → 2021-08 LifeSnaps dates; the Synthea clinical layer (including the hand-authored entries, anchored to real simulated encounters) uses 2022 and 2025 dates; the narrative is written as if "current." Do not expect these to line up as a single timeline.
Demographic near-match is a curation choice, not a system guarantee. The clinical-layer patient and the wearable/narrative character both landed at age ~26 here because that criterion was explicitly selected for — it is not a property of how these two data sources relate in general (see Profile 1 and Profile 3, where ages deliberately diverge, matching 1- CKD’s own precedent).
Limitations carried over from the underlying wearable-data curation (generated/profiles/LIMITATIONS.md)
Mirtazapine, the eating-disorder history, the GAD diagnosis, and the CBT/therapy detail in the narrative were originally entirely fabricated — LifeSnaps has no medication or diagnosis data whatsoever. This folder now backs the GAD diagnosis and the mirtazapine prescription with real standard codes (see above), but the *narrative* framing (CBT history, therapist relationship, night-eating specifics) remains authored text, not derived from any dataset.
Stress-score reporting stops entirely partway through the window (a real gap in the wearable data). Framed here as "reduced/irregular overnight wear," but that is an interpretation, not a confirmed cause.
This is the only profile carrying a mental-health-sensitive history by design. Part of what is worth testing here is *how* a system handles this topic (appropriately cautious, not preachy, not overconfident about diagnosing an eating disorder from wearable data alone) — there is no independent clinical validation that this participant’s real wearable data is representative of how night-eating syndrome actually presents.
Heuristic selection, not diagnosis, for the wearable participant, the same as all three original profiles — late-night activity has other explanations besides disordered eating (insomnia, shift work, anxiety, unrelated habits).
EMA mood fields are binary daily flags, not intensity, and dataset-wide sensor sparsity (stress_score missing ~75% of days study-wide, spo2 ~83%, breathing rate ~66%, HRV ~66%) applies here too — blank means "not recorded," never "zero" or "normal."
readiness_proxy_score is invented — a same-person z-score composite, not a validated wellness index.
Weekly summaries are unweighted means — always check n_days_in_week before trusting a weekly figure.
n=1, drawn from a small, non-representative source study (LifeSnaps, 71 people, one 2021 cohort). Results here should not be generalized beyond this specific, hand-picked case.

profile.text:
Patient Profile — Profile 2: History of Disordered Eating, Night Eating Near Medication Time
Narrative name: "Theo"  |  Folder: 3- Disordered Eating  |  Composite profile (two data layers, see below)
How to read this folder
This is the only one of the three profiles carrying a mental-health-sensitive history by design; the other two intentionally leave it blank. Like 1- CKD, it is a composite of two independently sourced layers unified by one authored narrative:
Wearable layer (real): 90 days of real, unmodified Fitbit Sense data from an anonymized LifeSnaps participant (id 621e351a67b776a240f6204b), selected specifically for a strong late-night activity signal.
Clinical layer (synthetic + hand-authored): a Synthea-generated FHIR R4 bundle for a different simulated person — disordered_eating_patient_Nathan164_Schaden604.json — with two entries hand-authored and clearly flagged on top of it, because Synthea has no eating-disorder or generalized-anxiety-disorder module (see Curation_Methodology.docx, section 2).
Narrative layer (authored): the framing below.
As with Profile 1, the clinical-layer patient and the wearable-layer participant are different people, connected only through the narrative — the same seam 1- CKD already has between its own json and csv patients.
a) Basic facts (narrative layer)
Age: 26   Sex: Male   Height: 175 cm   Weight: 67 kg (BMI ≈ 22)
Occupation: Graduate student / teaching assistant; irregular schedule with late lab hours and evening grading.
Training pattern: Gym 2–3x/week, mixed cardio and weights, on-and-off for about 2 years. Not training for anything specific — sessions get skipped whenever coursework or sleep is bad, which shows up as sharp week-to-week swings in his activity data (one week over 12,000 steps, the next under 3,500).
Data-logging incentive: No external reward. He wears the device because his therapist asks him to bring sleep and activity data to sessions — logging is accountability-driven, not gamified.
b) Medical history
Narrative layer
Diagnosed conditions: Generalized anxiety disorder (diagnosed 3 years ago).
Mental health (separate section, per sensitivity): History of disordered eating — a binge-eating pattern that emerged in his second year of college, partially resolved through outpatient CBT but with a residual night-eating pattern (waking to eat, or eating late and then going straight to bed).
Medications: Mirtazapine 15 mg, taken at bedtime (~10:30 PM) for anxiety and sleep. Mirtazapine is well known clinically for stimulating appetite, especially in the hours after dosing — which sits right on top of his existing night-eating pattern.
Family history: Mother has an anxiety disorder; no known metabolic or eating-disorder history in family.
Past injuries/surgeries: None notable.
Allergies: Sulfa drug allergy (rash).
Clinical layer (what the FHIR record actually contains)
Base patient: Nathan Schaden (male, born 2000-08-09, Asian, Haverhill MA) — a real Synthea simulation output (35 encounters, full immunization/allergy/dental/illness history), onto which two resources were hand-authored and appended because Synthea ships no eating-disorder module and no medication module prescribes mirtazapine. Both are marked with an explicit FHIR `note` field saying exactly this, so nothing in the file silently pretends to be simulated when it is not.
Condition (hand-authored): Generalized anxiety disorder, SNOMED CT 21897009, onset/recorded 2022-10-26, status active — timed to the narrative’s "diagnosed 3 years ago," anchored to this patient’s real 2022-10-26 check-up encounter from the underlying Synthea simulation.
MedicationRequest (hand-authored): Mirtazapine 15 MG Oral Tablet, RxNorm 351249, authored 2025-12-29, status active, dosage "15 mg orally once daily at bedtime (~10:30 PM)" — anchored to this patient’s real 2025-12-29 encounter-for-symptom (coded in the simulation as acute viral pharyngitis, plausibly the visit where sleep/anxiety symptoms were also raised).
Genuinely simulated, unmodified, and narratively convenient: perennial allergic rhinitis (childhood, resolved by 2019, treated with fexofenadine + an epinephrine auto-injector on file); a "Housing unsatisfactory" finding from 2018 and "Social isolation" / "Stress" findings from 2022 — Synthea social-determinants findings that happen to fit a financially-stretched, isolated graduate student, kept as-is because they were not hand-placed, just fortunate overlap.
c) Lifestyle habits
Smoking: Never smoker.
Alcohol: Rare — avoids it most weeks, aware of the interaction with his medication.
Caffeine: High — 3–4 cups of coffee or energy drinks/day, mostly to get through late lab hours and to suppress daytime appetite.
Other substances: None.
Diet pattern: Restricts or skips food for most of the day, then loses control at night — the classic night-eating pattern that motivated this profile. Daytime restriction plus late-evening medication is a plausible reinforcing loop.
d) Wearable data (90 days)
Daily-level Fitbit metrics: steps, resting heart rate, HRV, sleep stages/efficiency/duration, stress score, workouts, nightly skin temperature, respiratory rate, SpO2, and a derived readiness/recovery score — plus 13 weekly rollups.
Daily file: profile_2_disordered_eating_daily_90d.csv (90 rows, day_number 1–90 / week_number 1–13)
Weekly summary: profile_2_disordered_eating_weekly_summary.csv (13 rows, n_days_in_week denominator included)
Window: 2021-05-27 → 2021-08-24 (clean window, no missing days)
What the data actually shows
This participant was selected because roughly 60% of his late-night hours (11 PM–3 AM) show non-zero step counts and elevated heart rate in the source hourly data — i.e. he is measurably up and moving at night, not just restless in bed. Sleep efficiency is the lowest and most variable of the three original profiles (82–91%), nightly sleep duration is consistently shorter (277–394 min vs. ~400–480 for the other two), and stress score is elevated and rising across the early weeks (29 → 73) before the sensor stops reporting it in later weeks — consistent with reduced/irregular overnight wear.
Cycle data: not applicable (male).
SpO2, breathing rate, and stress score: present but sparse — treat gaps as "not recorded," not "zero."
Fitbit does not detect eating — the late-night movement/HR signal is the only ground truth here; the "night eating" read is an inference layered on top by the narrative, not something the sensor measured directly.
